original_value: Previous research on verbal representations shows how the news media consistently depicts young people’s uses of digital media in a narrow, negative light. In this article, we present an innovative methodology for demonstrating how young people and their digital practices are visually depicted. We focus on stock photography produced by the commercial image banks which source the news media with much of its imagery. Following an indicative analysis of news media images, we present a social semiotic analysis (grounded also in a descriptive content analysis) of a dataset of 600 stock photos top-sliced from three major image banks. By pinpointing dominant representational, compositional and interpersonal meanings, we show how image banks and, in turn, the news media produce a rather pessimistic metadiscursive framing of ‘teens and technology’. These influential visualizations are often reductionistic – consistently centering technologies over relationships; they are also problematic in, for example, their inexplicably gendered and classist assumptions.

result.paraphrase: Prior research on verbal representations indicates that news media consistently portrays young people’s digital media use in a narrow, negative way. In this article, we introduce an innovative method for showing how young people and their digital practices are visually represented. We concentrate on stock photography created by commercial image banks, which supply much of the news media’s imagery. After an indicative analysis of news media images, we conduct a social semiotic analysis, grounded in descriptive content analysis, of 600 stock photos sampled from three major image banks. By identifying dominant representational, compositional, and interpersonal meanings, we demonstrate how image banks and, in turn, the news media construct a rather pessimistic metadiscursive framing of “teens and technology.” These influential visualizations are often reductionist, repeatedly privileging technologies over relationships; they are also problematic in, for instance, their inexplicably gendered and classist assumptions.
